To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
'Elevated temperature, elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide and their combination increase crown respiration of 20-year-old Scots pine trees by 35, 16 and 27% respectively'.

(1) the increase in foliage mass and the change in the distribution of nitrogen in the crown of the trees caused by the EC treatment were the main factors responsible for the rise in crown respiration; (2) the increase in the ambient temperature caused a rise in crown resiration; and (3), the change in Q10 values of individual leaves, caused by the EC and ET treatments, had only a minor influence on the daily and the annual course of crown respirations.
'Elevated CO2 concentration and temperature both increased crown respiration of 20-year-old Scots pine trees, but the effects of elevated temperature were larger.'
In summary, our research is concerned with
the acclimation to EC and ET of respiration by foliage in the crown, and with the modelling of this acclimation.
the acclimation of respiration to increased temperature and CO2 in the crown of trees, and the modelling of the effects on annual crown respiration.

how the acclimation of respiration of Scots pines is related to the changes in the crown structure and microclimate, and how the acclimations of respiration of the individual leaves are extrapolated to predict the acclimation response of the whole crown.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of elevated CO2 concentration and temperature on respiration of Scots pines are mainly caused by the increase in foliage mass and the increase in ambient temperature, respectively, but that the changes in crown architecture, nitrogen distribution and respiration parameters of individual leaves induced by treatments are of secondary importance for crown respiration.

the effects of EC, ET and ECT on annual crown respiration of the 20-year-old Scots pine trees in the current experiment are mainly caused by the increase in the foliage area and the change in temperature, with only a minor contribution of changed respiration parameters for the individual leaves.
EC led to a slight decrease in R1.d(10) and a slight increase in Q10, ET and ECT led to a slight increase in R1.d.(20) and a decrease in Q10.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the increase in crown respiration due to elevated CO2 concentration is almost entirely attributable to the increase of foliage area.
EC, ET and ECT increased annual crown respiration by 16, 35 and 27%, respectively, but the contribution of changes in respiration parameters of individual leaves to annual crown respiration is small.
the effects of CO2 and temperature on respiration of individual needles were additive.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in addition to the increase in the foliage area, the changes in crown structure, and the corresponding changes in microclimate, are also important in the acclimation of respiration to elevated CO2 and temperature.
, in the future, increased foliage area will contribute more to the increase of crown respiration than the increase in ambient temperature and CO2 concentration.

the effects of increased CO2 concentration on the annual respiration of Scots pines are dominated by the increase in foliage biomass, whereas the effects of temperature are more evenly spread among the three components of crown respiration.
